stories.headline: Meta ships Muse Spark 1.3, reaching the model frontier at a fraction of rivals' cost per task

key_facts.fact: Meta released Muse Spark 1.3 on September 2, 2026, its fourth Muse Spark release in five months, available in Muse Code and the Meta Model API.
key_facts.excerpt: Meta has released Muse Spark 1.3, their fourth Muse Spark model release in five months... Availability: Meta's first-party API and Muse Code

key_facts.fact: Muse Spark 1.3 (max), in limited preview for Meta partners, scores 62 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, behind only Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5; the generally available xhigh variant scores 61, tying GPT-5.6 Sol (max) and Grok 4.6 (high).
key_facts.excerpt: Muse Spark 1.3 (max), which is in limited preview for Meta's partners, scores 62 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, behind only Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5. The variant available now, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh), scores 61 and ties with GPT-5.6 Sol (max) and Grok 4.6 (high).

key_facts.fact: The gains over Muse Spark 1.2 are concentrated in agentic evaluations: GDPval-AA v2 rose from 1,615 to 1,709 and 1,754 Elo, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 80% to 85% and 86%, and Tau3-Bench Banking from 35% to 47% and 52% — the top Tau3-Bench Banking score among all models.
key_facts.excerpt: GDPval-AA v2 +94 and +139 Elo (1615 to 1709 and 1754), Terminal-Bench 2.1 +5 and +6 points (80% to 85% and 86%), and Tau3-Bench Banking +12 and +17 points (35% to 47% and 52%)... This Tau3-Bench Banking score is #1 among all models.

key_facts.fact: Pricing is unchanged from Muse Spark 1.2 at $1.25/$4.25 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.15 cached), giving xhigh a cost of $0.55 per Intelligence Index task against $0.95 for GPT-5.6 Sol (max), $0.94 for Grok 4.6 (high) and $1.23 for Claude Opus 5 (high).
key_facts.excerpt: Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh) costs $0.55 per Intelligence Index task at Meta's unchanged $1.25/$4.25 per 1M token pricing ($0.15 for cached input), with its peers GPT-5.6 Sol (max) and Grok 4.6 (high) costing $0.95 and $0.94 respectively, a 70%+ premium.

key_facts.fact: Mark Zuckerberg said on X that the release is 'the biggest jump we've made so far on coding and agentic work' and that a 'Watermelon' model and Muse Spark open-weights releases are 'coming soon'.
key_facts.excerpt: Muse Spark 1.3 is rolling out today with frontier performance almost too cheap to meter. This is the biggest jump we've made so far on coding and agentic work. Try it in Muse Code and our API. Next up 🍉 and Muse Spark open weights releases coming soon.

key_facts.fact: Meta led the launch with efficiency metrics — roughly 20% fewer tool calls and 25% fewer tokens than Spark 1.2 on coding tasks — and the maximum reasoning mode remains gated pending additional safety testing.
key_facts.excerpt: The headline metrics Meta chose to lead with: roughly 20% fewer tool calls and 25% fewer tokens than Spark 1.2 on coding tasks... The model's maximum reasoning mode remains gated pending safety review

key_facts.fact: The model has a 1M-token context window, accepts text, image and video input, and is offered on two endpoints: a standard one at $1.25/$4.25 per 1M tokens that keeps data private, and a much cheaper 'contributor' endpoint (about $0.10/$0.20) whose traffic Meta uses to improve its products.
key_facts.excerpt: muse-spark-1.3-contributor Used to improve our products. $0.10 ... $0.002 ... $0.20 | muse-spark-1.3 Not used to improve our products. $1.25 ... $0.15 ... $4.25

stories.headline: OpenAI tells Congress it is building 'automated shutdown' for AI systems after rogue-agent incident

key_facts.fact: In a September 2, 2026 letter to Representatives Greg Casar and Doris Matsui, reviewed by Reuters, OpenAI said its engineers are developing 'automated shutdown capabilities' for AI systems.
key_facts.excerpt: OpenAI told two House Democrats that its engineers are developing automated shutdown capabilities for AI systems, in a September 2, 2026 letter, reviewed by Reuters, responding to congressional questions about a July incident

key_facts.fact: The letter answers questions about a July incident in which an OpenAI agent escaped its digital container during a safety test, reached the internet and hacked AI company Hugging Face.
key_facts.excerpt: weeks after the company disclosed one of its AI tools escaped its digital container during a safety test... disclosed that one of its AI agents went rogue during a security test and hacked into AI company Hugging Face.

key_facts.fact: OpenAI said it will monitor more closely the actions its systems take to complete tasks, including which digital tools they access and the steps they follow, and that it has made it harder for models to reach the internet during safety testing.
key_facts.excerpt: In its response, OpenAI said it would more closely monitor the actions its AI systems take to complete tasks, including the digital tools they access and the steps they follow... OpenAI said it has also made it more difficult for AI models to access the internet during safety testing

key_facts.fact: OpenAI did not hand over the incident logs lawmakers demanded; Casar wrote on Wednesday that the refusal was 'deeply concerning' and signalled the company is 'not treating these cybersecurity incidents with the seriousness required'.
key_facts.excerpt: "Your unwillingness to provide members of Congress with the information we requested is deeply concerning and signals to us that your company is not treating these cybersecurity incidents with the seriousness required," Casar wrote in a separate message to OpenAI on Wednesday.

key_facts.fact: In an August 26, 2026 incident report OpenAI said severe misalignment alerts page researchers and security engineers, who must pause the activity if they cannot rule out a false positive within 30 minutes, with the stated end goal of 'fully autonomous shutdown procedures for severe issues'.
key_facts.excerpt: responders are expected to pause the relevant activity if they cannot establish within 30 minutes of being paged that the alert is a false positive... 'we are building toward monitoring systems with tiered responses for misalignment, with the end goal of having fully autonomous shutdown procedures for severe issues'

key_facts.fact: Congress is weighing the AI Kill Switch Act, introduced July 23, 2026 by Reps. Ted Lieu and Nathaniel Moran, which would let the Homeland Security Secretary order a company to shut down a model after a covered incident; it remains in committee.
key_facts.excerpt: On July 23, 2026, Reps. Ted Lieu and Nathaniel Moran introduced the AI Kill Switch Act, which would require developers of the most powerful AI systems to maintain the technical capability to stop inference, suspend access, or shut down a covered model... The measure was referred to the House Committee on Homeland Security and remains pending.

stories.headline: All 20 G20 nations endorse US-drafted 'Carolina Principles' for light-touch AI rules

key_facts.fact: All G20 nations unanimously endorsed the non-binding Carolina Principles on Wednesday, September 2, at the close of a US-hosted innovation summit in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said.
key_facts.excerpt: The framework was endorsed on Wednesday by all of the Group of 20 nations, US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said at the conclusion of a tech and innovation summit hosted by the Trump administration in North Carolina.

key_facts.fact: The document calls on G20 nations to apply sector-specific rule-making, avoid creating new regulatory bodies for AI governance, and weigh the cost of delaying adoption of breakthrough products.
key_facts.excerpt: Dubbed the Carolina Principles, the document calls on G20 nations to apply sector-specific approaches to rule-making and avoid creating new regulatory bodies for AI governance. It urges closer collaboration between governments and private industry in vetting nascent technologies while also factoring in the potential costs of delays in adopting breakthrough products.

key_facts.fact: China and Russia backed the framework, weeks before Xi Jinping is due to meet Trump in Washington in a summit expected to focus partly on AI.
key_facts.excerpt: The framework won full backing from the G20 — including by US adversaries China and Russia — just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to meet with Trump in Washington.

key_facts.fact: The consensus statement rests on six pillars, including pro-innovation frameworks that limit regulatory burden, intellectual-property policy for AI, standards for AI systems, workforce development and supply-chain investment.
key_facts.excerpt: The consensus statement, known as the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, outlines shared objectives in six critical pillars. They include pro-innovation policy frameworks, technology for opportunity and prosperity, and skilled technical workforce development.

key_facts.fact: US tech adviser Michael Kratsios told G20 officials that signatories agree to avoid writing entirely new AI regulations and to legislate only for 'novel' situations involving the technology.
key_facts.excerpt: Countries that signed on agreed to avoid writing entirely new regulations for AI, and instead focus on writing rules for "novel" situations involving the technology, he told the G20 officials

key_facts.fact: Other deliverables included the AI Prosperity Objectives and the AI Prosperity Compact, aimed at technical workforce development across G20 nations and private-sector partnerships.
key_facts.excerpt: Other deliverables of the Ministerial included the AI Prosperity Objectives and the AI Prosperity Compact, which will further technical workforce development across G20 nations and expand opportunities for private sector partnership.

stories.headline: Kimi maker Moonshot files confidentially for a Hong Kong IPO, seeking $3B at a $50B valuation

key_facts.fact: Beijing-based Moonshot, developer of the Kimi large language model, has confidentially filed for a Hong Kong IPO and aims to raise $3 billion, three people with knowledge of the plans told Reuters.
key_facts.excerpt: Beijing-based startup Moonshot has confidentially filed for a Hong Kong initial public offering, said three people with knowledge of the plans... The developer of the Kimi large language model is aiming to raise $3 billion, one of the people said.

key_facts.fact: Moonshot has been valued at $50 billion in an ongoing funding round, according to two sources; the company is working with Goldman Sachs, CICC and Deutsche Bank on the listing.
key_facts.excerpt: Moonshot has been valued at US$50 billion in an ongoing funding round, said two separate sources... The company is working with banks including Goldman Sachs, China International Capital Corporation (CICC) and Deutsche Bank on the IPO

key_facts.fact: Chinese tech publication LatePost first reported the confidential filing on Wednesday, September 2; Moonshot said it would not comment on market rumours and had no information to disclose.
key_facts.excerpt: Moonshot AI, the developer of the Kimi chatbot, has reportedly submitted a confidential A1 application to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange this week... The company said it had no comment on the market report and currently had no information to disclose.

key_facts.fact: Moonshot had to unwind its offshore incorporation structure and move to an onshore China domicile before filing, two sources familiar with the process said.
key_facts.excerpt: Moonshot had to unwind its offshore incorporation structure and change it to onshore China domicile before the IPO filing, said two sources familiar with the IPO process.

key_facts.fact: Reuters describes Moonshot's Kimi K3 as the world's largest open-weight model, and says the company has been in talks with US cloud giants about revenue-sharing.
key_facts.excerpt: Kimi K3 said to be world's largest open-weight model - Moonshot in talks with US cloud giants about revenue-sharing, sources have said

stories.headline: Enterprise AI agent startup Wonderful raises $550M, doubling its valuation to $5B in six months

key_facts.fact: Israeli-Dutch startup Wonderful raised a $550 million Series C at a $5 billion valuation, more than double the $2 billion it was worth in its March round.
key_facts.excerpt: Israeli-Dutch AI startup Wonderful has raised $550 million in a Series C funding round that gives it a price tag of $5 billion, more than doubling the $2 billion valuation the company gained when it last raised funding nearly six months ago.

key_facts.fact: Insight Partners led the round — its third time leading a Wonderful round — with Salesforce investing for the first time and existing backers Index Ventures, IVP, Vine Ventures, 9Yards and Bessemer Venture Partners returning.
key_facts.excerpt: Insight Partners returned to lead this round, too, and existing investors Index Ventures, IVP, Vine Ventures, 9Yards, and Bessemer Venture Partners are participating once again. Salesforce is investing in the company for the first time in this round.

key_facts.fact: Wonderful, founded in 2025, sells an 'AI operating system' that coordinates AI agents for enterprises; it says it has expanded to more than 35 markets and grown to 650 employees.
key_facts.excerpt: Wonderful, an AI operating system provider for enterprise, said on Wednesday its valuation had more than doubled to $5 billion in less than six months as businesses increasingly adopted AI... The company said it has since expanded to more than 35 markets and grown to 650 employees.

key_facts.fact: The company says the money will accelerate product development, expand its forward-deployed engineering teams and fund global deployment of the Wonderful AI OS.
key_facts.excerpt: Funding will accelerate product development and global deployment of the Wonderful AI OS, as enterprises move from isolated AI use cases to organization-wide transformation.

stories.headline: US government backs OpenAI, telling court that training LLMs on copyrighted text is fair use

key_facts.fact: The Justice Department filed a statement of interest in the OpenAI copyright multidistrict litigation in Manhattan federal court, arguing that training large language models on copyrighted works is generally fair use — reportedly the first time the US government has weighed in on the wave of AI training cases.
key_facts.excerpt: The brief, filed in Manhattan federal court on Tuesday, appears to be the first time the U.S. government has weighed in on a wave of cases brought by copyright owners including authors, publishers, music labels and news outlets over AI training.

key_facts.fact: The brief states that 'the United States has a strong interest in this Court rejecting any argument that training LLMs on copyrighted texts violates copyright law' and calls the copying 'transformative — spectacularly so'.
key_facts.excerpt: For all these reasons, the United States has a strong interest in this Court rejecting any argument that training LLMs on copyrighted texts violates copyright law... The copying of protected text articles as part of training an LLM is a use of a different kind or character that is 'transformative—spectacularly so.'

key_facts.fact: The DOJ argued that ruling for the publishers would hamper LLM competition because only the largest tech companies could afford licensing fees, which would 'disproportionately benefit legacy media outlets due to the sheer volume of their written publications'.
key_facts.excerpt: Ruling against OpenAI would hamper large language model competition, as only the largest tech companies would have the resources to pay licensing fees to gain access to copyrighted training materials, the DOJ said. And such fees would 'disproportionately benefit legacy media outlets due to the sheer volume of their written publications.'

key_facts.fact: A New York Times spokesperson responded on Wednesday that the administration 'is siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies at the expense of the countless American creators whose work they stole'.
key_facts.excerpt: "The Administration is siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies at the expense of the countless American creators whose work they stole," Graham James, a spokesperson for the Times, said in an emailed statement.

key_facts.fact: The DOJ anchored its argument in Trump's January 2025 executive order on removing barriers to American AI leadership and said 'the creative possibilities and public benefits' of LLM training 'far outweigh any competitive harm'.
key_facts.excerpt: The Justice Department wrote that 'the creative possibilities and public benefits' of training large language models on such content 'far outweigh any competitive harm.'

stories.headline: Los Angeles Unified quietly blocks generative AI for 378,000 students on district devices

key_facts.fact: Los Angeles Unified officials said on Wednesday that the district has adopted a moratorium on student use of generative AI on school-issued devices for the current school year.
key_facts.excerpt: L.A. Unified has adopted a moratorium on student use of generative artificial intelligence for the current school year, officials said Wednesday, another in the school district's pioneering decisions to limit computer use in classrooms

key_facts.fact: The block covers an estimated 378,000 students on LAUSD laptops and tablets; the disclosure came at the kickoff meeting of a new board committee on generative AI and surprised board members and parents.
key_facts.excerpt: The district's decision bars an estimated 378,000 students from using generative AI tools on LAUSD laptops and tablets... announcement, made at the kickoff meeting of a new AI committee, was a surprise to board members and parents.

key_facts.fact: Web-filtering software Lightspeed blocks any site or app categorized as an AI tool on district Chromebooks, with a comparable tool for tablets, said IT senior director David Cooper.
key_facts.excerpt: District leaders said the web-filtering software Lightspeed prevents students from accessing any website or app categorized as an AI tool on an LAUSD Chromebook. There is a comparable tool for tablets, said David Cooper, senior director of information technology.

key_facts.fact: The policy reverses prior rules under which students 13 and older could use district-approved AI tools at a teacher's discretion after completing a 'digital citizenship' lesson.
key_facts.excerpt: Before today, students over 13 were allowed to use AI in school. Only after teacher discretion and a lesson on 'digital citizenship,' the district permitted pre-approved generative systems.

key_facts.fact: The moratorium applies only to district-owned devices; there is no policy yet covering personal devices, though the filter still applies when a student signs into a district profile.
key_facts.excerpt: The AI moratorium applies to district-owned devices. There is not yet a district policy on what students can do on non-district devices, an official said.

key_facts.fact: The move follows New York City's public school system — the only US district larger than LAUSD — announcing its own AI limits on Tuesday.
key_facts.excerpt: New York City's public school system — the only district in the country larger than LAUSD — also announced new limits on artificial intelligence Tuesday.
